meta.title: Who really said "Adventure is worthwhile in itself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: "Adventure is worthwhile in itself" is everywhere credited to Amelia Earhart — but no book, letter, or speech has been shown to contain it. Here’s what’s documented.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Adventure is worthwhile in itself'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Amelia Earhart and on her estate’s own site, yet tied to no documented source. An honest look at a much-loved but unsourced line.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Earhart — it even appears on her estate’s official licensing site ↗ — and it fits her adventuring temperament. But no primary source pins the exact wording: it is not in her 1928 memoir 20 Hrs., 40 Min., and it is absent from Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗. Treat it as genuinely attributed but undocumented.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None established — no book, letter, speech, or diary confirmed
The unsourced “decision to act … paper tigers” passage

trail: Searched the full Project Gutenberg text of Earhart’s first book, 20 Hrs., 40 Min. (1928) ↗ — the phrase does not appear.
The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Amelia Earhart page ↗ in every section (sourced, disputed, and misattributed).
It does appear on the official Amelia Earhart licensing site ↗ — but with no book, date, or citation attached.
It commonly rides on the tail of the unsourced “decision to act … paper tigers” passage, as on this widely shared essay ↗, which itself cites no source.
source.excerptNote: Online the line is usually presented alone, but it also circulates welded to the end of a longer passage — “The most difficult thing is the decision to act, the rest is merely tenacity. The fears are paper tigers … the process is its own reward. Adventure is worthwhile in itself.” That longer passage is itself undocumented, so the pairing lends the short line no real provenance.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording cannot be tied to any documented Earhart work, so no first-publication date can be established and no public-domain status can be asserted. Even the works sometimes loosely named for it — The Fun of It (1932) and Last Flight (1937) — would post-date 1931 and remain in copyright; but neither has been confirmed to contain the line.

author.name: Amelia Earhart

author.heading: Amelia Earhart
author.bio: Amelia Mary Earhart (1897–1937) was an American aviator and writer — the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and a tireless promoter of aviation and of women in flight. She was also a genuine author, publishing 20 Hrs., 40 Min. (1928) and The Fun of It (1932), with Last Flight assembled posthumously in 1937. Her real prose is plentiful and searchable, which is exactly why an undocumented one-liner like this one stands out.

misattribution.heading: An attribution without a source
misattribution.intro: The credit to Earhart is plausible and near-universal, but the paper trail is missing — and the line is often propped up by a second quote that is no better documented.

items.why: The line is printed on quote sites and even her estate’s licensing page ↗ with no book, letter, or date, and it does not appear in Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗ or in the full text of her 1928 memoir 20 Hrs., 40 Min. ↗

items.scope: The longer passage it rides on
items.why: The line is frequently appended to “The most difficult thing is the decision to act … The fears are paper tigers … the process is its own reward,” a passage that Wikiquote traces only to Earhart’s own website ↗ — not to any primary source — and whose self-help register reads as much later than her 1930s prose

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: genuinely Earhart-flavored and endorsed by her estate, but no speech, book, letter, or diary has yet been shown to contain the words — see Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, where it does not appear.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to pin down
lead: Earhart is a magnet for uplifting quotes because she left real, quotable writing — two books in her lifetime and a posthumous third — and because her life embodies daring. That combination makes a short, punchy line like “Adventure is worthwhile in itself” feel unimpeachably hers, even when no one can name the page it came from.

The tell here is the company it keeps: online it is usually fused to the “decision to act … paper tigers” passage, a piece of polished motivational prose that is itself undocumented. When an unsourced line is used to authenticate another unsourced line, the citation chain is circular — which is why we mark this attributed rather than verified.
context.pull: Credited everywhere, sourced nowhere — a beloved line still waiting for its page number.
